summary: Describes a technique for sending radio pages through Internet mail infrastructure, focusing on pagers identified by international telephone numbers. It documents technical procedures for the TPC.INT subdomain. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1703 describes how to send a one-way text message to a radio pager using ordinary Internet mail. It turns the pager's telephone number into a domain name, so that the mail system finds a paging server by the same rules it uses for any other domain. The paging server reads the address to work out which paging network to send through and which pager to send to.

subtitle: How to reach a radio pager by email, by turning the pager's telephone number into a tpc.int domain name.

tldr.problem: Radio paging is a one-way text service, and the people who wanted to send pages had no way to do it over the Internet mail infrastructure already in place.
tldr.mechanism: The memo turns a pager's telephone number into a domain name by reversing the digits and placing them under tpc.int, then addresses mail to a paging server with a local part that names the paging network and the pager.
tldr.outcome: Paging becomes an ordinary mail transaction: the message is routed by MX records like any other mail, and the paging server turns the mail body into a radio page.

facts.label: Recommended local-part length
facts.value: No more than 70 or so characters

today: RFC 1703 is an Informational memo published in October 1994, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets out the technical procedures for paging over Internet mail through the TPC.INT subdomain.

sections.title: Purpose of the Technique
sections.content:
As an adjunct to the usual two-way electronic mail service, it is at times useful to employ a one-way text notification service called radio paging. This memo describes a technique for radio paging that uses the Internet mail infrastructure, and focuses on the case in which radio pagers are identified through the international telephone network.

The technique, which maps telephone numbers to domain names, is derived from the TPC.INT subdomain. The general principles and policy for that subdomain are set out in RFC 1530; this memo covers the technical procedures that follow from them.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo describes how to send a one-way text message to a radio pager using ordinary Internet mail. The trick it uses is to turn the pager's telephone number into a domain name, so that mail routing finds the right paging server.

sections.title: Turning a Telephone Number into a Domain Name
sections.content:
A radio pager is identified by a telephone number, for example +1 415 940 8776, where +1 indicates the IDDD country code and the remaining string is a number within that country. A PIN may also be required to identify a particular radio pager uniquely.

The number is used to construct the address of a radio paging server, and that address is the recipient address of the message. Three forms are given: pager.ATOM@6.7.7.8.0.4.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int, pager-alpha.ATOM@6.7.7.8.0.4.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int and pager-numeric@6.7.7.8.0.4.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int. Here ATOM is an RFC 822 atom, an opaque string used for recipient identification when communicating with the paging network. The domain part is constructed by reversing the telephone number, converting each digit to a domain label, and placing the result under tpc.int. The telephone number used must not include any international access codes.

The memo notes that the mailbox syntax is purposefully restricted in the interests of pragmatism, and that some Internet mail software, especially gateways from outside the Internet, imposes stringent limits on the size of a mailbox string, so originating user agents should take care to limit the local part to no more than 70 or so characters.
sections.plainLanguage: The pager's telephone number becomes the domain name, read backwards one digit at a time. A prefix in the local part says what kind of pager it is, and the rest of the local part names the paging network or the pager itself.

sections.title: Routing with MX Records and Wildcards
sections.content:
The message is routed in exactly the same fashion as all other electronic mail, using the MX algorithm. Because a radio paging server may be able to access many radio pagers, the wildcarding facilities of DNS are used accordingly. A server at dbc.mtview.ca.us willing to access any radio pager with the telephone number prefix +1 415 940 might be published as the resource record *.0.4.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int. IN MX 10 dbc.mtview.ca.us.

If several radio paging servers were willing to access any radio pager in that prefix, multiple MX resource records would be present. The DNS servers for the TPC.INT subdomain perform a rudimentary form of load balancing by rotating the order of the MX records returned on each query.

The memo also points out that the presence of a wildcard record which matches a radio paging server's address does not imply that the corresponding telephone number is valid, or that a radio pager is identified by that phone number. The presence of the wildcard record indicates only that a radio paging server is willing to attempt access.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail for a pager is routed by the DNS MX records, exactly like mail for any other domain. A wildcard record lets one paging server offer to serve a whole block of telephone numbers, and several such records give the DNS servers something to choose between.

sections.title: What the Paging Server Does with the Address
sections.content:
To send information to a radio pager, the user application constructs an RFC 822 message containing a Message-ID field and a textual content, for example a text/plain content. The message is sent to the radio paging server's electronic mail address, and the server begins by looking at the local part of that address.

If the local part is either pager.ATOM or pager-alpha.ATOM, the recipient is using an alpha-numeric radio pager, and ATOM is read according to three rules. If ATOM consists entirely of numeric characters, it is a PIN, and the domain part refers to the IXO access telephone number for a radio paging carrier. Otherwise, if ATOM does not contain a hyphen, it is a CARRIER: a local database is consulted to determine the corresponding IXO access telephone number, and the telephone number corresponding to the domain part identifies the radio pager. If ATOM does contain a hyphen, everything to the left of the first hyphen is the CARRIER and everything to the right of it is the PIN.

If the local part starts with pager., the message sent to the radio pager consists of the body of the message. If it starts with pager-alpha., the radio paging server decides which information in the headers and body is used when constructing the paging message: some servers examine the To and Subject fields in addition to the body, while others simply send the body verbatim.

If the local part is the literal string pager-numeric, the recipient is using a numeric pager, and the radio pager dials the telephone number corresponding to the domain part. The message body must consist solely of digits.
sections.plainLanguage: The paging server reads the local part of the address to learn three things: whether the pager shows text or only digits, which paging network to send through, and which pager to send to. Whether the page text is just the body of the mail or also some of its headers is left to the server.

sections.title: Latency and the Choice of SMTP Command
sections.content:
An SMTP client communicating with a radio paging server may attempt either the MAIL command or the SEND command. The radio paging server must support MAIL, and may support any of SEND, SOML or SAML. The commands differ in what a positive completion reply to the RCPT and DATA commands means. With MAIL, it indicates at least that the message has been queued for transmission into the radio paging network. With SEND, it indicates that the radio paging network has accepted the message for delivery to the recipient. With SOML or SAML, it indicates that the message may have been accepted for delivery.

The IP level of the Internet performs datagram store-and-forward service, but gives end system hosts the appearance of direct connectivity. The Internet electronic mail service adds another layer of store-and-forward indirection, so that messages may go through any number of relays or gateways, and this may introduce delays of minutes, hours or days. A client that configures its Internet attachment to permit direct SMTP connectivity to a radio paging server submits paging requests without additional SMTP relaying, so the transmission from client to server is one SMTP hop and the Internet itself cannot add non-deterministic delay.

The combination of allowing direct IP and SMTP level interaction and using the SEND or SAML commands only means that a client receiving a positive reply from the server is assured that the page has been sent on the radio paging network. The memo notes that the primary constraints on this assurance are the server implementation and the client to server network connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary mail commands only promise that the page is waiting to be sent, while the SEND command promises that the paging network has taken it. To get that stronger promise without long delays, the client must reach the paging server directly instead of handing the message to relay servers on the way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section of the memo notes that Internet mail may be subject to monitoring by third parties, and in particular by message relays. It states nothing further about the security of the paging procedure, and requires no protection of its own beyond that warning.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who relays the mail along the way can read it. The memo warns about that and adds no other protection to the paging procedure.
